name: Karl Marx
info: Karl Marx (1818–1883) was a German philosopher, journalist and revolutionary socialist who, with Friedrich Engels, wrote The Communist Manifesto and developed a critique of capitalism in Das Kapital, ideas that gave rise to Marxism.

facts.born: 5 May 1818 at Brückengasse 664, Trier, then in the Kingdom of Prussia; third of nine children of Heinrich Marx, a lawyer, and Henriette Pressburg, a Dutch Jew from a prosperous business family; the family had converted from Judaism to Christianity before his birth
facts.died: 14 March 1883 in London, of bronchitis and pleurisy, aged 64 and stateless; buried on 17 March 1883 in Highgate Cemetery
facts.role: Doctor of philosophy, University of Jena (1841); editor of the Rheinische Zeitung (1842–1843) and the Neue Rheinische Zeitung (1848–1849); member of the Communist League; European correspondent of the New-York Daily Tribune (1852–1862); member of the General Council of the International Workingmen's Association (from 1864)
facts.known: The Communist Manifesto (1848, with Friedrich Engels); Das Kapital (volume I, 1867); historical materialism; the analysis of class struggle, alienation and surplus value; the Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875); his part in the First International; Marxism

t: Born in Trier to a lawyer's family that had converted from Judaism, Marx studied law and philosophy, took a doctorate at Jena in 1841 and became a radical journalist, expelled in turn from Prussia, France and Belgium.

With Friedrich Engels he wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848, then spent the rest of his life in London, where he worked on Das Kapital, whose first volume appeared in 1867, and helped lead the First International.

His followers debated how to interpret him, revolutions in many countries called themselves Marxist, and his legacy is still contested: opponents blame him for deaths in those states, while others separate his ideas from what was later done in his name.
dyk: When Marx died in 1883 he left a personal estate valued for probate at £250, and only between nine and eleven mourners, by Francis Wheen's count, attended his funeral at Highgate Cemetery.
ev: Born in Trier in the Kingdom of Prussia
Awarded his doctorate by the University of Jena for a thesis on Democritean and Epicurean philosophy of nature
Marries Jenny von Westphalen and moves to Paris to co-edit the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher
The Communist Manifesto is first published on 21 February; Marx then returns to Cologne and founds the Neue Rheinische Zeitung
Ordered to leave Prussia, expelled from Paris and settled in London, where he remains for the rest of his life
Elected to the General Council of the International Workingmen's Association at its inception
The first volume of Das Kapital is published
Dies in London on 14 March and is buried in Highgate Cemetery

sections.early:
Karl Marx was born on 5 May 1818 to Heinrich Marx and Henriette Pressburg at Brückengasse 664 in Trier, then part of the Kingdom of Prussia. The family was originally non-religious Jewish but had converted to Christianity before his birth; his paternal line had supplied Trier's rabbis since 1723. After Prussia's annexation of the Rhineland in 1815 and the abrogation of Jewish emancipation, his father, a lawyer, converted to the state Evangelical Church of Prussia in order to retain his career. Heinrich Marx was a man of the Enlightenment and a classical liberal who took part in agitation for a constitution. Karl was the third of nine children and became the eldest son when his brother Moritz died in 1819. He and his surviving siblings were baptised into the Lutheran Church on 28 August 1824.

He was educated privately by his father until 1830, when he entered the Gymnasium zu Trier, whose headmaster, Hugo Wyttenbach, employed many liberal humanists as teachers. In 1832 police raided the school and discovered literature promoting political liberalism among the students. In October 1835, at 16, Marx went to the University of Bonn wishing to study philosophy and literature, but his father insisted on law as more practical. He was excused from military duty because of a "weak chest". At Bonn he joined the Poets' Club, whose political radicals were monitored by the police, and the Trier Tavern Club; in August 1836 he took part in a duel. His grades deteriorated and his father forced a transfer to the University of Berlin.
sections.rise:
In Berlin, Marx enrolled in the law school in October 1836 but was fascinated by philosophy and became interested in Hegel, whose ideas were then widely debated. Through the Doctors Club he became involved in 1837 with the Young Hegelians, gathered around Ludwig Feuerbach and Bruno Bauer, who adopted Hegel's dialectical method to criticise established society, politics and religion from a left-wing perspective. He had become engaged to Jenny von Westphalen, a member of the petty nobility who had known him since childhood. His father died in May 1838, which diminished the family's income.

He completed his doctoral thesis, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature, in 1841. Because it was controversial among conservative professors at Berlin, he submitted it to the more liberal University of Jena, whose faculty awarded him the degree in April 1841. An academic career was barred by the government's growing opposition to classical liberalism and the Young Hegelians, so in 1842 he moved to Cologne and became a journalist on the radical Rheinische Zeitung. Prussian censors checked every issue. After the paper published an article strongly criticising the Russian monarchy, Tsar Nicholas I requested a ban and Prussia's government complied in 1843.

Marx married Jenny on 19 June 1843 in Kreuznach, seven years after their engagement, and that October the couple moved to Paris, where he had become co-editor of the Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher with Arnold Ruge.
sections.deeds:
In Paris Marx studied political economy and the French socialists and, between April and August 1844, wrote the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts, which treat alienated labour. On 28 August 1844 he met Friedrich Engels at the Café de la Régence, beginning a lifelong friendship. In 1845, at the request of the Prussian king, the French government shut down the paper Vorwärts! and François Guizot expelled Marx from France. He moved to Brussels, where he and Engels wrote The German Ideology, which was not published in his lifetime but only in 1932, and where he wrote The Poverty of Philosophy (1847) in reply to Proudhon.

In June 1847 the League of the Just was reorganised as the open Communist League, and Marx and Engels took part in drawing up its programme. They wrote The Communist Manifesto from December 1847 to January 1848; it was first published on 21 February 1848. After the Revolutions of 1848 began, Marx was arrested by the Belgian authorities, who accused him of using part of an inheritance to arm Belgian workers, an allegation whose veracity is disputed. He fled to France, then went to Cologne, where on 1 June he began the daily Neue Rheinische Zeitung. He was tried several times and acquitted each time, but the paper was suppressed and he was ordered to leave Prussia on 16 May 1849.

In London from 1849 he lived in extreme poverty and depended largely on Engels. From 1852 to 1862 he was European correspondent of the New-York Daily Tribune. In 1859 he published A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy, and in 1864 he was elected to the General Council of the First International. The first volume of Das Kapital appeared in 1867.
sections.opponents:
Marx's quarrels were frequent. His friendship with Arnold Ruge broke down over the Jahrbücher. In 1850 the Communist League split when August Willich and Karl Schapper urged an immediate uprising; Marx and Engels called this "adventuristic", and Marx's view prevailed in the League, though he lost the same contest in the German Workers' Educational Society and resigned from it on 17 September 1850. In the First International he fought the anarchists led by Mikhail Bakunin. According to Engels, the Neue Rheinische Zeitung remained "a simple dictatorship by Marx". The biographer Werner Blumenberg wrote that his verdicts on enemies and friends alike were sometimes harsh enough to give offence.

Some of his writings have been disputed. His essay "On the Jewish Question" has been described as evidence of antisemitic views by Paul Johnson, Bernard Lewis, Hyam Maccoby and Robert S. Wistrich, a reading disputed by Wendy Brown, Robert Fine, David McLellan and Francis Wheen, among others. In the Neue Rheinische Zeitung of February 1849 he and Engels called for "the most determined use of terror" against the Slav peoples they regarded as counter-revolutionary. On India, he wrote that Britain was "the unconscious tool of history" in bringing a social revolution; the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy says this can sound like a rationalisation of foreign domination, but reflects his ambivalence towards capitalism.

Critics have called his emphasis on the primacy of social relations economic determinism. Political opponents in countries associated with Marxism have blamed him for millions of deaths, while others argue for a distinction between his own influence and that of those who shaped his ideas for political purposes.
sections.last:
In the last decade of his life Marx's health declined and he became incapable of the sustained effort of earlier years, though he still commented on contemporary politics, particularly in Germany and Russia. His Critique of the Gotha Programme (1875) opposed the tendency of Wilhelm Liebknecht and August Bebel to compromise with the state socialist ideas of Ferdinand Lassalle, and contains the phrase "From each according to his ability, to each according to his need". In a letter to Vera Zasulich dated 8 March 1881 he considered the possibility that Russia might bypass the capitalist stage and build communism on the common ownership of land in the village mir, provided that the influences assailing it were first eliminated. Volumes II and III of Das Kapital remained manuscripts on which he worked for the rest of his life.

His wife Jenny died in December 1881, and he developed a catarrh that kept him in ill health for the last 15 months of his life. His eldest daughter died in January 1883. The catarrh brought on the bronchitis and pleurisy that killed him in London on 14 March 1883, when he was 64 and stateless. According to Engels, he was found in his armchair, "peacefully gone to sleep". He was buried on 17 March in Highgate Cemetery in an area reserved for agnostics and atheists; Engels and Liebknecht were among those who spoke. His estate was valued at £250. Engels edited and published volume II of Das Kapital in 1885 and volume III in October 1894.
sections.legacy:
Marx's ideas had a profound impact on world politics and thought, in particular after the 1917 Russian Revolution. His followers have debated how to interpret him, and the legacy has become contested among tendencies that each see themselves as his most accurate interpreter, among them Leninism, Marxism–Leninism, Trotskyism, Maoism and Luxemburgism. Throughout the 20th century revolutions in dozens of countries labelled themselves Marxist, most notably the Russian Revolution, which led to the founding of the Soviet Union. Leaders such as Lenin, Mao Zedong, Fidel Castro and Josip Broz Tito have cited him as an influence.

His work contributed to the birth of modern sociology: Isaiah Berlin considers him the true founder of modern sociology "in so far as anyone can claim the title", and Karl Löwith considered Marx and Søren Kierkegaard the two greatest philosophical successors of Hegel. Historians inspired by his social theory include E. P. Thompson and Eric Hobsbawm, who remarked that "one cannot say Marx died a failure"; Antonio Gramsci sought to understand transformative political practice in its light. Marx's family was reburied on a new site in Highgate in November 1954, with a tomb unveiled on 14 March 1956 bearing the last line of the Manifesto.

Chemnitz was named Karl-Marx-Stadt after him. In May 2018 a statue of him by the Chinese sculptor Wu Weishan, donated by the Chinese government, was unveiled in Trier. In 2013 UNESCO added two documents in his handwriting to its Memory of the World International Register: his annotated first edition of Das Kapital, volume I, and a manuscript page of the Manifesto.

summary: Karl Marx (1818–1883), born in Trier, was a German philosopher and journalist who, with Friedrich Engels, wrote The Communist Manifesto in 1848 and, in London, the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867. His ideas, known as Marxism, inspired revolutions and parties in many countries, and his legacy remains contested.
references: Saul Kussiel Padover, Karl Marx, an intimate biography (McGraw-Hill, 1978)
Isaiah Berlin, Karl Marx: His Life and Environment (Oxford University Press, 1963)
Werner Blumenberg, Karl Marx: An Illustrated Biography (Verso Books, 2000)
Michael Heinrich, Karl Marx and the Birth of Modern Society: The Life of Marx and the Development of His Work. Volume I: 1818–1841 (Monthly Review P., 2019)
Eric Hobsbawm, How to Change the World: Tales of Marx and Marxism (Little, Brown, 2011)
notes: Fact checks: the article's 'dictatorship by Marx' remark is Engels's own, attributed as such. The 'Slav peoples' sentence quotes the 1849 Neue Rheinische Zeitung passage jointly signed by Marx and Engels; the article says Marx considered Slavic nations except Poles counter-revolutionary and notes Engels held a similar sentiment.
The Belgian arms allegation: the article says Marx 'allegedly' used a third of an inheritance of either 6,000 or 5,000 francs and that the allegation's veracity is disputed; the figures are left out.
Move to London: the article says Marx moved in 'early June 1849' in one place and 'August 1849' in the Cologne section; the text says only 1849.
The article says Marx was 'stateless' at death but does not say when he lost nationality; left as given.

Left out: the Freddy Demuth paternity allegation (disputed, no documented evidence), his health and retrodiagnosis, the Darwin and Tremaux passages, the Algeria passage, the films and the long list of leaders and theories named in the legacy sections, Engels's 'greatest living thinker' remark (praise, not given). The article's Philips family details were also left out.
Legacy section cites the article's own attributed judgements (Berlin, Löwith, Hobsbawm); the article calls him 'one of the most influential figures of the modern era', which is not repeated.
